Host/disease context: Plum pox virus causes sharka in Prunus and is an established phytosanitary pathogen of stone fruits.
Vector/transmission context: Potyviruses are transmitted predominantly by aphids in a non-persistent, non-circulative manner.
Representative official/curated source: EPPO PPV000; IPPC Diagnostic Protocol DP 2 (Plum pox virus)

Host/disease context: Cherry leaf roll virus is associated with leaf roll, mosaic and ringspot disease contexts; nepovirus host range varies from broad to restricted among species.
Vector/transmission context: Many nepoviruses are transmitted by longidorid nematodes; seed and/or pollen transmission is also common.

Representative documented virus or disea: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus (Begomovirus coheni)
Host/disease context: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus is an EPPO-listed tomato pathogen; begomoviruses collectively infect a wide range of dicotyledonous plants.
Vector/transmission context: Begomoviruses are transmitted by the whitefly Bemisia tabaci species complex.
Representative official/curated source: EPPO TYLCV0; IPPC UK pest-status report for tomato yellow vein streak begomovirus

Host/disease context: Cowpea mild mottle virus is documented from multiple cultivated hosts including legumes and tomato and is associated with mottle, chlorosis and necrosis disease phenotypes.
Vector/transmission context: Cowpea mild mottle virus is transmitted by Bemisia tabaci; non-persistent whitefly transmission has been reported for this member.
Representative official/curated source: EPPO CPMMV0 datasheet and vector record
Representative biology reference: Jeyanandarajah & Brunt, 1993, DOI 10.1111/j.1439-0434.1993.tb01334.x; Chang et al., 2013, PMID 30722532

Host/disease context: Pepino mosaic virus has a relatively broad documented host range, with Solanaceae as the principal host group and tomato as an important crop host.
Vector/transmission context: Natural transmission of potexviruses is primarily by mechanical contact; Potato aucuba mosaic virus can be aphid-transmitted when assisted by a potyvirus helper protein.

Host/disease context: Cucumber mosaic virus has an exceptionally broad host range spanning numerous cultivated and wild plant species.
Vector/transmission context: Cucumoviruses are transmitted by aphids in a non-persistent manner.

Host/disease context: Potato leafroll virus is a major potato pathogen associated with leaf roll and phloem-limited disease.
Vector/transmission context: Poleroviruses are transmitted by specific aphids in a persistent, circulative and non-propagative manner.
Representative official/curated source: EPPO PLRV00; IPPC UK pest-status report for non-European PLRV isolates

Host/disease context: Tomato spotted wilt virus has a broad host range and affects major food and ornamental crops.
Vector/transmission context: Orthotospoviruses are transmitted by thrips in a persistent, propagative manner.

Host/disease context: Cacao swollen shoot disease is caused by a complex of badnaviruses and represents a major cacao disease context.
Vector/transmission context: Badnaviruses are transmitted semi-persistently by mealybugs and, for some members, by aphids or lace bugs; they do not multiply in the mealybug vector.

Representative documented virus or disea: American plum line pattern virus (Ilarvirus APLPV)
Host/disease context: American plum line pattern virus is an EPPO A1-listed ilarvirus associated with line-pattern disease of plum.
Vector/transmission context: Ilarviruses are pollen-associated; thrips can mediate mechanical transmission when feeding on virus-bearing pollen.

Host/disease context: Fabaviruses have wide host ranges and can cause ringspot, mottling, mosaic, distortion, wilting and apical necrosis.
Vector/transmission context: Fabaviruses are transmitted by aphids in a non-persistent manner.

Host/disease context: Rice tungro spherical virus participates in the economically damaging rice tungro disease complex; waikavirus host ranges are usually restricted to a few plant families.
Vector/transmission context: Waikaviruses are transmitted semi-persistently by aphids or leafhoppers; rice tungro spherical virus is leafhopper-transmitted.
